extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, judges, and legal scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the quality of a patent's nonobviousness showing (both prosecution record and issued patent) with special attention to hindsight bias and doctrinal changes after KSR. Emphasizes procedural safeguards and substantive evidence that make an obviousness determination hindsight-resistant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindsight-Resistant Procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct prior art baseline before viewing the claimed invention; document specific reasons combining references would have been motivated absent hindsight; identify what teaching, suggestion, or motivation existed in the prior art at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural steps to reduce hindsight: (a) reconstruct the relevant prior-art landscape before disclosing the invention; (b) explicitly record why a POSITA would combine references (motivations) without reference to the invention; (c) identify teaching, suggestion, or motivation actually present in the art at the relevant time. Emphasizes that these steps should be done before or independently of the inventor's disclosure to avoid bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. John Deere Discipline (core obviousness factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Graham factors without invention bias: (1) scope and content of the prior art (without invention bias); (2) differences between prior art and claims (carefully delineated); (3) level of ordinary skill (calibrated to actual practitioners); (4) secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain discipline in each Graham factor: do not let knowledge of the invention color the claimed 'scope and content' analysis; precisely delineate claim elements vis-à-vis references; calibrate the POSITA to realistic practitioners (not idealized or hindsight-amplified skill); preserve and evaluate secondary indicia as potentially dispositive evidence of nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR Application Limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obvious to try" requires limited, identified, predictable solutions; "common sense" must be supported by evidence, not bare assertion; combination must be predictable to POSITA, not just possible in retrospect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under KSR, courts accept more flexible rationales but quality analysis should demand: (a) demonstration that the options were limited and that one of ordinary skill would have been reasonably expected to try the claimed solution with a reasonable expectation of success; (b) evidentiary support for any invocation of 'common sense'—not mere conclusory statements; (c) focus on predictability to a POSITA rather than post-hoc plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Markers in the Patent Itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification distinguishes the invention from each cited reference with technical reasons; claims include specific limitations the prior art does not teach; secondary-considerations evidence (commercial success, copying, etc.) is preserved in the record; prior-art search was thorough, leaving few blindspots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete signs of a robust nonobviousness showing: detailed specification explanations differentiating over cited art, claim drafting that incorporates technically substantive limitations (not merely formalistic language), preservation of secondary indicia in the file history and record, and documentation (or indicia) of a thorough prior-art search during prosecution to reduce unknown references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Defects Indicating Vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim differences from prior art are minor or framed in conclusory terms; no technical justification for novel limitations; prosecution history shows applicant arguments unsupported by specification; specification reads as a rationalization of the prior art combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags that a patent is likely to be invalidated for obviousness: superficial or conclusory claim distinctions, absence of technical explanation for claimed features, reliance in prosecution on arguments not grounded in the specification, and specifications that appear to be post-hoc rationalizations rather than contemporaneous technical justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative Test — Prior Art Universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Was the relevant prior art comprehensively considered during prosecution?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the scope and completeness of the prior-art universe addressed in prosecution: whether searches were conducted and documented, whether relevant categories of art were considered, and whether examiner-cited or applicant-disclosed references fairly represent the contemporaneous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative Test — Claim Differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the claim differences from prior art technically substantive, not merely formal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claim limitations correspond to concrete technical distinctions that the prior art does not teach or suggest; beware of sleight-of-hand claim drafting that purports to 'add' limitations without technical substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative Test — Motivation Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there an articulated reason the POSITA would NOT have arrived at the claimed combination?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit articulation (in prosecution or record) of why a POSITA would be discouraged from combining the references or why the combination was non-obvious—this can include evidence of contrary teachings, incompatibilities, or technical unpredictability at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative Test — Secondary Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the record include unexpected results, commercial success, copying, long-felt need, or other secondary indicia?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether secondary indicia are preserved and supported with evidence in the record; these factors can corroborate nonobviousness and help guard against hindsight reasoning, so their preservation and documentation during prosecution are quality markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative Test — Hindsight Resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the claims survive analysis when the examiner reconstructs the prior-art landscape without reference to the invention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform a counterfactual reconstruction: would a fact-finder, ignorant of the invention, have been led to combine the references? A robust patent should survive this exercise; failure indicates susceptibility to hindsight bias and potential invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-KSR (TSM) Historical Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-KSR: strict TSM (teaching-suggestion-motivation) test required explicit references-based motivation, which tended to lower hindsight risk because explicit motivation was required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note useful for comparative evaluation: patents prosecuted and examined under a strict TSM regime may have different record expectations (explicit motivations in references) than those after KSR; when evaluating older patents, consider the doctrinal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-KSR Quality Requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-KSR environment requires explicit teaching against the claimed combination (negative motivation); specific technical reasons the combination is non-trivial; documented unexpected results; and strong secondary-considerations evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because KSR permits 'common sense' and 'obvious to try' rationales, high-quality patents in the post-KSR era should: (a) identify any prior art teaching away from the combination, (b) provide technical explanations showing non-triviality, (c) document unexpected results when available, and (d) preserve secondary indicia to bolster nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operative Principle — Affirmatively Counteract Hindsight Bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonobviousness analysis is systematically biased toward invalidity due to hindsight, and quality patent prosecution must affirmatively counteract this bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General evaluative principle: patents should not rely solely on the presumption of validity to withstand hindsight; instead, prosecution should actively build evidentiary support (prior-art baseline, documented motivations, technical justifications, and secondary indicia) so that the patent can survive scrutiny when the fact-finder's exposure to the invention risks skewing obviousness judgments.
